en: The UK favourites in the Alps
at the UK's favourite Alpine resorts

en.title: Powder watch at the UK's favourite Alpine resorts: up to 121 cm of new snow by 23 November
en.description: Val Thorens leads with 143 cm of fresh snow in 72 hours as of 20 November. Alpe d'Huez forecast to gain 121 cm by 23 November.
en.lede: Three days of heavy snowfall have buried the upper slopes across the UK's favourite Alpine resorts, with Val Thorens receiving the most: 143 cm in 72 hours. Alpe d'Huez is next in line to gain the most, with a forecast of 121 cm by 23 November.

sections.h: Which resort gets the most powder next
p: If you are planning a trip between now and 23 November, Alpe d'Huez will be the best bet. The forecast calls for 121 cm of new snow by then, on top of the 111 cm that fell in the last three days. That puts the resort at a strong starting point for a mid-week getaway.

Val Thorens and Courchevel follow, though with less gain ahead: 92 cm and 86 cm respectively by 23 November. Both have already picked up heavy falls, so the powder quality will depend on wind and temperature between now and your arrival.

sections.h: What fell in the last three days
p: Val Thorens topped all UK favourites with 143 cm in 72 hours to 20 November. Les Arcs and Chamonix were close behind at 134 cm and 133 cm. These three resorts are the best bets if you can get there within the next day or two, before the new snow settles and hardens.
Alpe d'Huez received 111 cm, Courchevel and Méribel 125 cm each. Even Avoriaz, the shallowest of the 12 resorts tracked, picked up 94 cm in three days.
All 12 resorts have snow on their upper slopes. Les Arcs holds the deepest base at 166 cm, followed by Val Thorens at 145 cm and La Plagne at 144 cm. The middle value across all resorts is 116 cm.
Alpe d'Huez sits at 130 cm, strong enough for confident skiing on most terrain. At the lower end, Avoriaz has 62 cm and Chamonix 99 cm, so check conditions on lower runs before heading there.

Powder lies mainly above 2,900 m across this region. Les Arcs and Alpe d'Huez reach 3,205 m and 3,306 m respectively, so their upper runs keep the snow longest. Val Thorens at 3,221 m and La Plagne at 3,058 m are equally reliable.
Chamonix's upper limit is 2,486 m, which means the fresh powder will soften faster as the day warms. Avoriaz at 2,250 m is best suited to early starts and shaded slopes.

Alpe d'Huez works well for a two or three-day visit. It has 130 cm now and will gain another 121 cm by 23 November, so you will ski into improving conditions rather than chasing melt. The transfer time from Geneva or Lyon is roughly three hours, leaving time to reach the slopes by afternoon.

Val Thorens demands a faster decision: it has the deepest snow (145 cm) and the most recent falls (143 cm), but the forecast shows only 92 cm more. If you go in the next 36 hours, you will catch the powder at its freshest.

After this much new snow, the upper slopes offer powder opportunities for those equipped and trained. Layers this thick can shift, so check the official avalanche bulletin for your chosen resort before heading beyond the marked runs.

A transceiver, shovel and probe are essential. Travel with a guide if you are not familiar with the terrain, and start early: the first few hours after a cold night give the best snow and the least sun-softening.

advice: Alpe d'Huez is the safest choice if you have a week: powder now and 121 cm more by 23 November.
Val Thorens and Chamonix need a faster trip: their recent falls (143 cm and 133 cm) are the draw, but the forecast shows less gain ahead.
Winter tyres or chains are essential for the final climb to these resorts, especially after three days of fresh snow.
Start before sunrise: cold overnight temperatures lock in the best texture, and the first runs are yours.
Off-piste only with the avalanche bulletin read and proper rescue gear carried.
